title: Food
intro: You can buy most of your fresh food without a supermarket. Edenvale has its own farmers market, and two big wholesale markets (City Deep and Springs) are open to the public. A few pots on a ground-floor patio can cover your herbs and greens most of the year.

sections.title: How food reaches Joburg
points: Most fresh fruit and veg goes through council-run wholesale markets. Farmers send produce there, agents sell it for them, and buyers pay the day's price.
Joburg Market in City Deep is the biggest of these. It calls itself the leading fresh produce market in Africa.
Prices change every day with supply. Good rains in 2026 brought more produce into the Springs market and pushed some prices down.

Quick context on supermarkets: four chains run formal grocery retail. In 2019 the Competition Commission found that their exclusive leases in malls kept smaller shops out. That's why buying around them takes a bit of effort.
Food is expensive right now. PMBEJD (a Pietermaritzburg research group) says its Joburg household food basket cost R5,766.71 in October 2026.
No VAT is charged on 21 basic foods, including brown bread, maize meal, eggs, dried beans, and fresh fruit and veg. Buying these loose and direct gets you the most value.

sections.title: Buying direct near Edenvale
points: Edenvale Farmers Market runs outside De Backery in the Edenvale CBD. It's on the first and last Saturday of each month, 07:00 to 12:00. Stalls sell veg, fruit, eggs and meat.
Anyone can buy at Joburg Market. Bring your ID and register at a customer service kiosk for a free buyer card. Load money onto it at the cashier, then buy from the agents in the halls.
For smaller amounts at Joburg Market, use the People's Market (the old Mandela Market). Traders there split bulk stock into smaller lots, and it's cash only.
The Ekurhuleni Fresh Produce Market in Springs is closer to home and open to everyone. You don't need to be a business. A market agent says prices are often better than in shops.
Bryanston Organic & Natural Market (40 Culross Road) has been running for about 40 years. Go there for certified-organic and specialty produce. It runs on Thursdays and Saturdays.
For meat, buy a whole lamb or a quarter beef from a farm or a butcher who buys direct, and have it cut and packed for the freezer. Ask where the animal came from and how it was raised.

sections.title: Veg boxes, co-ops and bulk buying
points: Delivery services cut out the supermarket too. Munching Mongoose delivers organic produce, grass-fed meat and dairy across greater Joburg, with no maximum order size.
Split a market haul with one or two other households. A pocket of onions or a box of tomatoes is cheap per kg but too much for two people.
Buy dry staples like rice, maize meal, lentils, oil and flour in bulk from a cash-and-carry. Always compare the price per kg, not the pack price.
Buy what's in season and cheap, then freeze it, sauce it or pickle it. A small chest freezer pays for itself if you buy meat in bulk.
Go early. Wholesale markets close by 10:00 or 11:00, and the best stock goes first.

sections.title: Growing your own in a rental
points: Grow in things you can move: grow bags, big pots, or a raised bed on legs. You keep the garden when you move, and the landlord's lawn stays untouched.
Johannesburg's last frost is usually mid-August and the first frost around mid-June. Plant tomatoes outside in October or November.
Start with easy, high-yield crops: Swiss chard (local 'spinach'), lettuce, radish, cherry tomatoes, bush beans, spring onions, basil and parsley. Give mint its own pot.
Give pots at least 6 hours of direct sun. Use bagged potting mix, not garden soil, and make sure water drains out the bottom.
Save water: mulch the soil, water early in the morning, and catch rain in a bucket during summer storms. Highveld winters are dry, so pots dry out fast.
A worm farm on the patio turns kitchen scraps into free fertiliser. A ready-made one with 500 worms costs about R2,700, or you can build one from stacked crates.

sections.title: Labels and ultra-processed food
points: Ingredients are listed from most to least by weight, so the first three tell you what you're really eating.

Ultra-processed food (UPF) is made with industrial ingredients you wouldn't cook with at home, like emulsifiers, flavourings, colourants and sweeteners. Fizzy drinks, packaged snacks and sugary cereals are typical examples.

A 2024 BMJ review covered almost 10 million people. It linked eating more UPF with 32 health harms, including heart disease deaths and type 2 diabetes. These studies show links, not proof of cause, but the pattern is consistent.
SA's planned front-of-pack warning labels (draft regulation R3337) were still not law in mid-2026. So turn the pack over and read the back.
Use the 'per 100g' column to compare products. Check sugar and sodium first.

do: Put the next first or last Saturday in the calendar for Edenvale Farmers Market (07:00 to 12:00, outside De Backery).
Go to Joburg Market once on a weekday before 09:00 with your ID. Register for the free buyer card and walk the People's Market.
Try the Springs market on a Saturday morning and compare prices with your last grocery slip.
Buy 3 large pots, potting mix and seedlings (Swiss chard, lettuce, basil, cherry tomato) this month. It's still summer planting season.
Start a worm farm, bought or DIY, and stop throwing veg scraps in the bin.
Set a monthly food budget and see how close you get to PMBEJD's R5,766 Joburg basket.
ask: What's in season and cheapest this week?
Where is your farm, and did you grow this or buy it in?
Do you spray? If so, with what?
Can I get a better price for a full box, pocket or crate?
For meat: how was the animal raised (grass-fed or feedlot), and can you cut and pack a quarter or half for the freezer?
Do you deliver to Edenvale, or is there a pickup point nearby?
watch_out: 'Farm fresh' on a market stall doesn't always mean the seller grew it. Some resell wholesale stock, so ask.
'Natural' and 'organic-style' are marketing words. Only certified organic has a standard behind it.
Bulk only saves money if you use it. A 10 kg box of tomatoes that rots costs more than 1 kg from a stall.
Market hours are early, and wholesale halls close by 10:00 or 11:00. Don't arrive at noon.
Don't fill pots with garden soil. It compacts and drowns roots, so use potting mix.
UPF research shows strong links but rarely proves cause. Eat more whole food without getting scared of every packet.

resources.title: Food Intelligence: The Science of How Food Both Nourishes and Harms Us
resources.why: A top US nutrition scientist and a health journalist sort out what the evidence really says about ultra-processed food and why we overeat.
takeaways: Published September 2025. Hall ran the landmark ultra-processed food feeding studies.
Explains how nutrients and metabolism actually work.
Covers how the food environment shapes what we eat.
Looks hard at blood-sugar tracking and 'precision nutrition' hype.

resources.title: The Cultural Politics of Food in South Africa: Media, Nourishment, Inequality
resources.source: Mehita Iqani & Sarah Gibson (Wits) — Manchester University Press
resources.access: Buy from the publisher (price not checked). Not free.
resources.why: A South African look at how history, media and inequality shape what ends up on local plates.
takeaways: Out March 2026, launched at Wits in September 2026.
Covers how colonialism, migration and apartheid shaped SA food.
Looks at how food culture reflects inequality in who eats well.

resources.title: Barons: Money, Power, and the Corruption of America's Food Industry
resources.access: Buy: Kindle or Takealot (price not checked)
resources.why: How a few firms came to control the food supply. A useful mirror for supermarket power in SA.
takeaways: Profiles seven US food giants and the families behind them, including Cargill, JBS and Walmart.
Shows how political influence and weak regulation helped them grow.
The cases are American, but the lessons about concentrated power carry over.

resources.title: Container Gardening: The Permaculture Way
resources.why: Written for patios and balconies, which suits a rental where you can't dig beds.
takeaways: Covers choosing containers, wind and sun.
Companion planting, small-scale composting and natural fertilisers.
Staggered harvests and which plants suit pots.

resources.title: High Yield, Small Space Organic Gardening
resources.why: Getting the most food from a small space, so it fits a ground-floor patio.
takeaways: Out April 2025.
Organic veg growing in small spaces.
Written for a US climate, so shift planting dates for Highveld frost and summer rain.

resources.title: The Johannesburg fresh produce market: its operations and contribution to the food system
resources.source: Malungane & Wegerif (University of Pretoria) — Frontiers in Sustainable Food Systems
resources.why: How City Deep, the market that feeds Joburg, actually works, and who you'd be buying from there.
takeaways: It's Africa's biggest fresh produce market by volume and turnover.
Based on 127 interviews and 60+ visits from 2019 to 2023.
Informal traders buy there and supply poorer neighbourhoods.
Ageing infrastructure and supermarkets buying straight from farms both threaten it.

resources.title: Fresh Produce Market Inquiry: Final Report
resources.why: The official answer on why fruit and veg cost what they do in SA supermarkets.
takeaways: Launched January 2025.
Names six competition problems, including inefficient municipal markets and market agents' conduct.
High supermarket mark-ups on some lines, but slim net margins after costs.
31 remedies, including more buying through the fresh produce markets.

resources.title: Dietary intake of low-income adults in South Africa: ultra-processed food consumption a cause for concern
resources.source: Frank, Swart, Ng et al. — Public Health Nutrition
resources.why: Real South African numbers on how much ultra-processed food people eat.
takeaways: 2,521 adults in Langa, Khayelitsha and Mount Frere.
Ultra-processed food was about 39% of the average diet.
Only 7% met the WHO fruit and veg target.

resources.title: Socioeconomic inequality in food consumption among households with women of childbearing age in South Africa
resources.source: Nglazi & Ataguba (UCT) — PLOS Global Public Health
resources.why: How income and where you live shape how much ultra-processed food a household buys.
takeaways: Uses national household spending surveys.
Poorer households spend a bigger share of income on food.
Income, race and living in a city explained most of the gap.

resources.title: Ultra-processed foods and human health: the main thesis and the evidence
resources.source: Monteiro, Baker et al. — The Lancet (series paper 1 of 3)
resources.access: Free to read with free Lancet registration
resources.why: The most authoritative recent summary of the ultra-processed food evidence, and its limits.
takeaways: Published November 2025, drawing on 43 experts.
Argues ultra-processed food is pushing out fresh and minimally processed diets.
Much of the evidence is observational, which the series acknowledges.
Backs front-of-pack warning labels and tighter marketing rules.

resources.title: BFAP Food Inflation Brief (December 2025 prices)
resources.source: Bureau for Food and Agricultural Policy (BFAP)
resources.why: What a basic healthy food basket costs in SA, so you can benchmark your own grocery bill.
takeaways: The Thrifty Healthy Food Basket averaged R3,899 in 2025, up 2.9% on 2024.
Meat had the highest food inflation in 2025, at 7%.
BFAP publishes these monthly.

resources.title: Edenvale Farmers Market
resources.why: First and last Saturday of the month, 07:00 to 12:00, outside De Backery, Edenvale CBD. Farm veg, eggs and meat, no entry fee.
takeaways: The April 2026 report places the market outside De Backery in Edenvale CBD.
It lists the first and last Saturday of each month, from 07:00 to 12:00.
There is no entrance fee and the format excludes entertainment programming and alcohol sales.
Fruit, vegetables, eggs and fresh or prepared meat vendors are welcomed.
Stalls were advertised at R50, with booking by SMS or WhatsApp rather than calls.
The article’s vendor rules exclude baked goods, drinks and ready food, so it describes a produce-focused market.

resources.title: How to buy at Joburg Market
resources.why: City Deep. Mon 05:00 to 10:00, Tue to Fri 05:00 to 11:00, Sat 05:00 to 10:00. Bring your ID for a free buyer card.
takeaways: The supplied short link did not load, but the operator’s linked How to Buy page was found and checked.
Bring identification and register at a customer-service kiosk in a produce hall.
The first buying card is free, with R50 stated for replacing a lost card.
Load funds with a cashier before purchasing through market agents.
The guide states no general minimum or maximum purchase quantity, although goods are sold in their available units.
Keep the issue receipts and arrange removal after each agent’s purchase rather than carrying bought stock between agents.

resources.title: People's Market and Unity Market at Joburg Market
resources.why: City Deep, same hours as the main market. Smaller quantities, cash only.
takeaways: The People’s Market was formerly called Mandela Market.
The operator describes more than 100 informal fruit and vegetable traders there.
It sells loose produce and smaller quantities for cash without a buying card.
Trading extends later than the main halls, towards lunchtime from Monday to Saturday.
Unity Market is behind the trading halls and has more than 50 mainly vegetable traders.
The page describes planned facilities, so its future-tense construction statements are not proof that those facilities have opened.

resources.title: Ekurhuleni Fresh Produce Market, Springs
resources.why: Springs, East Rand. Open to the public and running in 2026. Early mornings; Saturday is busy, so phone for exact hours.
takeaways: The city’s June 2026 release identifies the market as a regional wholesale hub in Springs.
It reports 15,000 square metres of trading space.
It lists 17 cold rooms and 24 ripening rooms, although the sentence’s wording is ambiguous about how those totals relate.
The city describes it as Gauteng’s third-largest government-owned fresh produce market.
The release links improved seasonal crop supply to lower customer prices.
Cashless trading and online shopping are described as plans, not confirmed operating services.

resources.title: Bryanston Organic & Natural Market
resources.why: 40 Culross Rd, Bryanston. Thursdays and Saturdays, mornings to mid-afternoon. Organic food; call 011 706 3671 to confirm hours.
takeaways: The tourism listing gives the address as 40 Culross Road, off Main Road, Bryanston.
It describes food alongside crafts, home decor, clothing and wellness products.
The market is a registered fundraising trust associated with Michael Mount Waldorf School.
Market profits support the school’s infrastructure and the international Waldorf education system.
The listing does not establish that every stall is an independently certified organic grower.
The supplied page does not state operating days, so confirm these through the market before travelling.

resources.title: Munching Mongoose
resources.why: Delivery across greater Joburg: organic produce, grass-fed meat, dairy and eggs.
takeaways: The current homepage describes an online grocer and offers combo boxes.
It lists separate categories for grass-fed meat and certified organic products.
It advertises expanded delivery days for greater Johannesburg.
It says deliveries use a cold chain and that there is no maximum order size.
Delivery-service information and buying policies are linked separately.
The homepage alone does not confirm an Edenvale delivery slot or a CSA arrangement that shares crop risk.

resources.title: Johannesburg planting calendar (Zone 9b)
resources.why: Month-by-month sowing and harvest chart. Frost from mid-June to mid-August.
takeaways: Fryd classifies Johannesburg as Zone 9b with a subtropical highland climate.
The guide gives mid-August as last frost and mid-June as first frost.
It suggests starting salad tomatoes indoors in August or September and transplanting in October or November.
Its lettuce guidance includes outdoor sowing from August to February.
It flags summer thunderstorms as a factor in watering decisions.
The same calendar is offered for several neighbouring cities, so its frost dates are broad estimates rather than a guarantee for Edenvale.

resources.title: Jane's Delicious Garden Planner
resources.why: Lay out containers or beds and get a planting calendar for your location. Jane is Joburg-based.
takeaways: The planner supports drawing beds, placing crops and changing the layout.
It generates a planting calendar personalised to location.
The described formats include containers, raised beds, rows and square-foot gardening.
The website also offers individual garden consultations in Greater Johannesburg.
This is planning software and a commercial service, rather than a tested promise about yields or financial savings.

resources.title: Livingseeds
resources.why: SA heirloom seed shop with seedlings (herbs from about R15) and garden supplies.
takeaways: The direct homepage could not be retrieved during this research, so these points use corroborating retailer and gardening descriptions.
Livingseeds is described as a South African family seed business specialising in heirloom and open-pollinated varieties.
Its catalogue also includes sprouting and microgreen supplies.
Published descriptions support seed-saving as a reason to choose stable open-pollinated varieties.
Current seed counts, catalogue size, opening hours and germination guarantees could not be verified from the supplied homepage.

resources.title: The Worm Oasis worm farm
resources.why: SA-made, about R2,717 with 500 worms. Fits on a patio.
takeaways: The listing describes a South African manufactured, UV-resistant worm farm.
It has two working trays and a separate drainage tray with a tap.
The package includes coco-coir bedding, instructions and about 500 composting worms.
Dimensions are listed as 42 cm wide, 52 cm deep and 49 cm high.
The retrieved price was R2,716.95 including VAT, with shipping calculated at checkout.
The seller promotes the collected liquid for garden use, but that claim does not establish that raw drainage liquid is safe to spray on edible leaves.

resources.title: Household Affordability Index (October 2026)
resources.why: Monthly cost of a household food basket. Joburg was R5,766.71 in October 2026.
takeaways: PMBEJD published the October 2026 index on 28 October 2026.
Its reported household food basket cost R5,512.53 that month.
Its separate basic nutritional basket for seven people cost R6,692.25.
The gap between those baskets was R1,179.72, about 18% of the nutritional basket’s cost.
The nutritional basket for seven increased by R218.35, or 3.4%, from October 2025.
This measures food affordability for larger low-income households rather than prescribing what a couple should spend.

resources.title: Grocery Retail Market Inquiry report (2019)
resources.why: The official look at how the big chains limit smaller competitors.
takeaways: UCT’s page is a brief library notice pointing to the Competition Commission’s report, rather than the report itself.
It is dated 29 November 2019.
The notice says grocery retail has strong potential for small-business participation.
It says features of the sector impede that participation.
The library notice alone does not provide detailed findings or evidence of current market shares, so those should be read in the linked report.

resources.title: The big question around SA's VAT-free food
resources.why: How the 21 zero-rated foods work and who benefits most.
takeaways: The article was published on 1 December 2024 and discusses a possible expansion of zero-rated foods.
It reports 21 zero-rated basic food items at that time.
It explains that richer households can receive larger rand benefits while poorer households receive larger benefits relative to income.
It summarises arguments that grants can target poverty more directly than further zero-rating.
It warns that tax relief may not be fully passed through to consumer prices.
Its R30 million estimate for existing revenue forgone is not substantiated here and should not be reused as a verified fiscal total.

resources.title: Ultra-processed food linked to 32 health harms
resources.why: Plain summary of the biggest UPF evidence review (2024).
takeaways: This BMJ press release describes 45 pooled analyses drawn from 14 review articles involving almost 10 million participants.
Higher ultra-processed food exposure was associated with 32 adverse health outcomes.
The release reports around 50% higher cardiovascular death risk and about 12% higher type 2 diabetes risk in the relevant analyses.
Evidence strength varied by outcome, with limited evidence for some cancers and gastrointestinal outcomes.
The authors acknowledge possible unmeasured influences and inconsistent ways of measuring food intake.
These relative-risk associations do not prove that one food caused an illness or predict an individual’s outcome.

resources.title: SA's draft food labelling regulations (R3337): current status
resources.why: Why warning labels still aren't on SA packs (July 2026).
takeaways: The legal explainer is dated 24 July 2026 and says R3337 remained draft.
It dates the draft’s publication for comment to April 2023.
The proposal includes front-of-pack warnings for specified nutrient thresholds and certain artificial sweeteners.
Products carrying warnings could face restrictions on health claims, endorsements and child-oriented promotional devices.
The author advises manufacturers to comply with R146 while the replacement text and timetable remain uncertain.
This is a dated legal interpretation, so the official regulations library is the reference for later changes.

resources.title: Jane's Delicious Garden
resources.why: The SA organic veg bible, covering nearly 100 veg and herbs. R370.
takeaways: The supplied ISBN is 9781920289935, listed as a 2017 Sunbird edition.
The listing describes practical preparation, planting and growing advice for vegetables and herbs.
Its scope ranges from small urban spaces to smallholdings.
It advertises guidance for nearly 100 vegetables and herbs.
The description mentions more than 200 photographs, step-by-step instructions and personal experience.
Only the listing and description were available, so these are scope takeaways rather than a full-book review.

resources.title: Jane's Delicious Urban Gardening
resources.why: Small-space growing: containers, edible walls, rainwater and grey water. R370.
takeaways: The supplied ISBN is corroborated by the publisher as Jane Griffiths’ urban gardening book published in September 2015.
It covers containers, edible walls, raised beds, rooftops and community growing spaces.
Small urban orchards and converting existing lawns are explicit topics.
It also covers hens, bees and aquaponics [growing plants with nutrients from an aquatic animal system].
Rainwater harvesting and grey-water reuse are included alongside gardening.
The scope is verified from the publisher description, while any particular water-reuse method still needs its own suitability check.

resources.title: Ultra-Processed People
resources.why: Readable, evidence-based guide to what UPF is and why it matters. R305.
takeaways: The listing frames the book as an investigation of food science, industrial production, economics and history.
Van Tulleken argues that food environments constrain choice rather than treating weight solely as failed willpower.
The account includes his personal experiment eating a diet high in ultra-processed food.
The book argues for a right to know what food contains and for access to affordable food.
The supplied paperback edition is listed as published on 2 May 2024.
A personal experiment illustrates a question but does not carry the evidential weight of a controlled trial.

resources.title: Food Rules: An Eater's Manual
resources.why: Short rules for eating simply, one per page. A quick read.
takeaways: Pollan presents one short rule per page with a concise explanation.
The book’s aim is to simplify everyday eating decisions amid conflicting advice.
It draws on food traditions from different cultures.
The author’s page links a PDF excerpt and contemporary reviews.
The supplied page describes a practical rule-based handbook rather than a systematic scientific review.
Its cultural rules should therefore be used as prompts for judgment rather than medical guarantees.

resources.title: How one woman sparked a suburban organic renaissance (TEDxJohannesburg)
resources.why: 16 minutes on why growing your own food in Joburg works.
takeaways: The indexed talk and transcript identify Jane Griffiths as the speaker and TEDxJohannesburg as the event.
She describes a long transition from travelling and adventure to growing food at home.
Growing chillies was a starting point before expanding to other vegetables.
She presents healthy soil and relationships among garden organisms as central to the garden.
Aphids and their predators illustrate the value of observation and ecological balance.
This is a personal gardening account, not a controlled comparison of organic and conventional diets.

resources.title: 10 Veggies to start in November in South Africa
resources.why: What to plant right now, from a current SA channel (Oct 2026).
takeaways: Verification gap: the supplied video could not be retrieved and an exact-ID search returned no result.
The provided title describes November planting, but no crop list could be checked.
The creator, publication date and intended South African climate zone remain unverified.
No sowing dates or crop recommendations are attributed to this video without accessible content.

resources.title: How to start a vegetable garden in pots
resources.why: SA container growing for renters (2026).
takeaways: Verification gap: the supplied video could not be retrieved and its exact ID produced no search result.
Only the user-provided title identifies it as a container-gardening tutorial.
Its container sizes, drainage instructions and growing-medium advice could not be checked.
Use the verified City of Cape Town container guidance in the new resources until this video’s content can be inspected.

resources.title: Worm Farms: How to really get them working
resources.why: Practical SA worm farm setup and troubleshooting.
takeaways: Indexed YouTube metadata identifies the creator as Livingseeds Farm and the publication date as 16 June 2022.
The description presents the video as troubleshooting for worm farms that are not functioning.
It links a separate tutorial about Activated Worm Effluent, abbreviated A.W.E.
A full transcript was not accessible, so no particular feeding ratio, temperature target or liquid-treatment method is asserted here.
The description alone does not demonstrate the safety or effectiveness of applying effluent to edible crops.

resources.title: Joburg Market: small-scale buyers making a living with fresh produce
resources.why: See how the market floor works before you go (2025).
takeaways: Verification gap: the supplied video did not load and an exact-ID search produced no result.
The user-provided title describes small-scale buyers at Joburg Market.
Its buyer interviews, prices and trading dates could not be checked.
No claims about savings or purchasing rules are attributed to it; the verified operator pages provide the usable buying guidance.

resources.title: The harsh reality of ultra-processed food
resources.why: Lecture version of the UPF evidence.
takeaways: YouTube identifies the talk as The harsh reality of ultra processed food with Chris van Tulleken.
The Royal Institution’s event description identifies the topic as the industrialisation and commercialisation of diets.
It describes his month-long personal experiment eating an 80% ultra-processed diet.
The talk’s stated scope includes appetite, health and the limits of relying on exercise and willpower alone.
It proposes responses by individuals and policymakers rather than only personal restraint.
The event description is accessible, but the full YouTube transcript was not retrieved, so detailed causal claims should be checked against the trials.

resources.title: Evidence-based natural pest control for SA gardens
resources.why: 4 minutes on dealing with pests without poisons.
takeaways: Verification gap: neither the supplied video nor an exact-ID search exposed accessible content.
The supplied title alone calls it evidence-based and South African.
The creator’s credentials, cited studies and suggested pest treatments could not be checked.
Do not treat the title as proof; the new UC IPM resource supplies verifiable guidance on aphids and natural enemies.

resources.title: Competition Commission proposes big changes to selling of fresh produce
resources.why: A readable account of the final inquiry and the mechanics of price transparency.
takeaways: The inquiry covered five fruit groups and six vegetables, rather than every food sold in South Africa.
Different pack sizes made like-for-like price comparisons difficult.
The report required named major retailers to add prices per 100 g for the 11 prioritised produce categories.
The report linked high mark-ups alongside slim net margins to costly supply chains.
The article also identifies municipal market inefficiency and high input costs as barriers.

resources.title: Market forces: Inquiry assesses the cause of price fluctuations
resources.why: Reporting from City Deep shows the people and transactions behind a market price.
takeaways: The report follows buyers collecting stock at Johannesburg’s City Deep market early in the morning.
It reports that about 5,000 farmers supply Joburg Market.
One buyer supplies West Rand shopkeepers who are themselves facing customer complaints about prices.
The market publishes a daily price list that the article says changes at noon.
This is reporting during the inquiry, so use the 2025 final report for its conclusions.

resources.title: Hawkers in dire straits
resources.source: Lesego Chepape and Mandisa Ndlovu, Mail & Guardian
resources.why: Local reporting from Tembisa explains affordability, small portions and traders’ losses.
takeaways: Maria Khoza had traded vegetables at Tembisa train station since 1992.
She sourced stock from wholesalers at Swazi Inn in Tembisa.
Her wholesale spinach bundle rose from R12 to R25, prompting her to sell smaller R10 bundles.
Another trader described R650 of fruit stock deteriorating before she could recover her investment.
These are reported 2023 experiences, not current price quotations or representative national averages.

resources.title: Three years, 6,000 pages, no labels: Who’s stalling SA’s food warnings?
resources.why: Investigates how the proposed warning labels moved through government and industry consultation.
takeaways: The Department of Health reported submissions from 179 companies and organisations totalling more than 6,000 pages.
A four-member technical team reviewed the material.
Nedlac’s task team first met for substantive engagement on 26 August 2026.
The department said it had amended the draft, but Priceless SA said it had not seen the revised text.
The article reports no firm publication date and several remaining legal and consultation steps.
Concern about possible industry self-regulation proposals is distinguished from verified knowledge of the current submission.

resources.title: Commentary on the Fresh Produce Market Inquiry report
resources.why: An informed second view that tests whether structural reforms will actually work.
takeaways: NAMC says many concerns repeat findings from its 2006 Section 7 investigation.
It supports reinvesting market profits in infrastructure, training and market access.
It argues that changing ownership models also needs internal management reform.
It warns that commission caps could produce hidden charges or poorer service.
It supports better price disclosure while recommending phased implementation and support for smaller sellers.

resources.title: NIH study finds heavily processed foods cause overeating and weight gain
resources.why: A clear introduction to the experiment that moved this debate beyond observational links.
takeaways: Twenty adults stayed at the NIH Clinical Center for a continuous month.
Each person received two weeks of each diet, with the order randomised.
Meals offered were matched on several nutrients, but participants chose how much to eat.
People ate about 500 extra calories daily on the ultra-processed diet and ate faster.
Average weight rose by 0.9 kg during that diet and fell by 0.9 kg during the minimally processed diet.

resources.title: Start a food garden
resources.why: Useful South African container and harvesting advice, with climate-specific limits.
takeaways: The guide recommends a sheltered growing site with ideally six hours of direct sun.
It describes making drainage holes in reused containers so water can escape.
Some vegetables need 30 to 45 cm of growing depth.
Harvesting outer lettuce or spinach leaves lets the plant continue producing.
Planting every two to three weeks can spread harvests over time.
Its stated climate is Cape Town’s wet-winter climate, so its seasonal advice needs adaptation for Edenvale.

resources.title: Composting at home
resources.why: Explains decomposition and the limits of products sold as instant composters.
takeaways: Composting is aerobic [oxygen-dependent] decomposition by microorganisms.
A working pile needs carbon-rich browns, nitrogen-rich greens, water and air.
Fruit scraps, dry leaves and suitable shredded cardboard are listed ingredients.
Meat, dairy and pet waste are excluded from the ordinary backyard approach described.
The guide includes worm composting as a separate household option.
Food-scrap grinders and dehydrators produce material for composting rather than finished compost.

resources.title: Food and input prices report library
resources.why: Bookmark the continuing monitoring series rather than relying on a single food-price headline.
takeaways: The library lists dated food and input price reports.
It includes March 2026 and December 2025 reports.
It also lists food-input cost policy advisory issues for June and September 2026.
The reports distinguish input-price pressures from prices paid for final food.
Check the observation period within each report because publication and price collection dates can differ.

resources.title: Food Control regulations library
resources.source: South African National Department of Health
resources.why: The official reference point for checking which food rules actually exist.
takeaways: The library lists R146 of 1 March 2010 under food labelling.
It links the 2010 and 2012 amendments to that framework.
It separately lists sodium-reduction rules and their amendments.
It separately lists the 2011 trans-fat regulations.
Pesticide and veterinary-drug controls use maximum residue limits [legal limits for residues in food].
A proposed warning-label regulation should be checked against official publication rather than treated as law because a campaign promotes it.

resources.title: Joburg Market daily price list
resources.why: A wholesale reference for planning pooled purchases and testing price claims.
takeaways: This is the market operator’s dedicated daily-price-list page.
It is a wholesale reference rather than an Edenvale home-delivery quotation.
The operator also links buyer registration and a directory of market agents.
The fetched page did not expose a readable commodity table, so no live R/kg prices are reproduced here.

resources.title: Joburg Market wholesalers directory
resources.why: Find actual tenants and store numbers before making a wholesale buying trip.
takeaways: The directory separates Halls 1 and 2, Hall 9, informal markets and the shopping complex.
It provides tenant names and store numbers rather than a single central shop.
Top Crop Wholesalers is listed at stores 118A/B and 119B.
AB Fresh Produce Distributors has several listed stores, including 116A/B and 117A/B.
The directory establishes location, but does not promise household minimum orders, prices or delivery.

resources.title: Bulk Veg ordering and delivery FAQ
resources.why: A produce delivery option that explicitly names Edenvale and nearby suburbs.
takeaways: The delivery list explicitly includes Edenvale, Bedfordview, Modderfontein and Kempton Park.
The page lists Tuesday and Friday deliveries from 08:00 to 18:00 and Saturday from 07:00 to 16:00.
Its advertised delivery table shows R25 for a stokvel basket of R75 or more and R35 for the lower-value category.
Orders can be placed online or through the contact methods listed on the page.
An invoice follows processing, with EFT and mobile-wallet payment options.
The business says most packaging is returnable; confirm current charges and route availability before ordering.

resources.title: Kleinhans Free Range Farm
resources.why: A Cullinan farm-direct meat lead with an explicit Johannesburg delivery schedule.
takeaways: The business identifies its farm location as Cullinan, Gauteng.
It advertises Johannesburg and Pretoria deliveries once a week.
It lists Cullinan and Rayton deliveries every second week.
Orders are placed online and delivery dates confirmed through WhatsApp.
The site says deliveries usually take place on Wednesdays and Thursdays between 08:00 and 17:00.
Its free-range and nutritional claims are seller statements, while exact Edenvale coverage and slaughter documentation still need confirmation.

resources.title: Farm Fresh Meat delivery and packaging FAQ
resources.why: A practical Gauteng meat supplier to compare with farm-direct offers.
takeaways: The supplier is based in Tedderfield Estates south of Johannesburg.
It advertises delivery anywhere in Gauteng at R125 per order.
Its stated lead time is two to four working days.
Customers can request particular packaging through the cart’s special-request section.
Concerns should be raised within 24 hours, with refusal of all or part of a delivery also described.
This FAQ establishes service terms, but does not by itself establish that every product comes from the seller’s own farm.

resources.title: Organic certification: understanding South Africa’s assurance systems
resources.why: Helps distinguish an organic claim from a documented verification process.
takeaways: First-party assurance is a farmer’s own claim supported by a direct relationship with the consumer.
PGS [participatory guarantee system] is second-party assurance involving farmers, consumers and other participants.
PGS groups conduct farm visits and can issue certificates to approved members.
Third-party certification uses an accredited independent body and is described for longer supply chains and exports.
An in-conversion seal distinguishes land still moving towards organic status.
PGS assurance does not mean the business is consumer-owned or that the food has passed a clinical nutrition trial.

resources.title: A Seed Saving Guide for Gardeners and Farmers
resources.source: Micaela Colley, John Navazio and Lisa DiPietro, Organic Seed Alliance
resources.why: A detailed practical reference on keeping varieties and seed quality over generations.
takeaways: Originally published in 2010, this guide was revised in 2026.
Stable open-pollinated varieties usually produce offspring resembling their parents when unwanted crossing is prevented.
Saving hybrid seed is generally discouraged when the goal is to preserve the original variety’s traits.
The crop chart concerns the final number of seed parents, not merely how many seedlings to sow.
The guide covers harvesting, cleaning, drying and storage as distinct stages.
Much of its experience comes from the US Pacific Northwest, so local growing seasons need adaptation.

resources.title: Jane’s Delicious A-Z of Vegetables
resources.why: A South African crop reference to consult one vegetable at a time.
takeaways: The listing identifies ISBN 9781920289973 and publication on 1 October 2017.
Its scope includes common vegetables and less familiar varieties available to South African growers.
It describes crop-specific sowing, planting, feeding and watering guidance.
Protection, harvesting and preparation are included alongside cultivation.
Seed saving is an explicit part of the book’s scope.
These points are verified from the publisher description on the listing, not a claim to have read the full book.

resources.title: The contribution of cart traders to fresh produce accessibility in Soshanguve township, South Africa
resources.source: Oscar Sithole and Marc C. A. Wegerif, Discover Food
resources.why: Gauteng fieldwork challenges assumptions that informal food trade is necessarily expensive.
takeaways: Published on 30 October 2025, the study uses fieldwork centred on Soshanguve with other Gauteng sites.
Researchers tracked eight produce items and found cart traders cheaper than the comparison supermarket.
For cabbage, potatoes, onions and tomatoes, supermarket prices were 28.7% to 112.3% higher in the comparisons reported.
Small portions included quarter cabbages and R5 potato packets.
Trust networks and occasional credit helped customers with limited cash.
This is a qualitative case study with local price observations, not proof of a permanent price advantage throughout South Africa.

resources.title: The 2024 Christmas Lectures: The truth about food
resources.why: Three illustrated lectures connect digestion, appetite and the food system.
takeaways: Lecture 1 follows food from sensory cues through the digestive tract.
The demonstrations include an endoscope and explanations of microbes in digestion.
Lecture 2 explains how cells extract energy and how food supplies material for body repair.
Lecture 3 examines the long history of processing and cooking before addressing modern industrial food.
The page embeds the lectures and provides substantial descriptions, so viewers outside Britain can use it without relying on BBC access.
Some demonstrations involve babies and family participation, which may affect when you want to watch.

resources.title: Horticultural zones
resources.source: South African National Biodiversity Institute, PlantZAfrica
resources.why: A South African check against relying on a generic overseas hardiness label.
takeaways: The site divides South African horticultural conditions into regional zones.
It identifies a summer-rainfall Karoo and Highveld zone.
It describes severe winter frost on the escarpment as a major restriction on outdoor plant choice.
Its Highveld zone includes a broad coldest-month minimum-temperature range from below -5°C to 5°C.
This regional framework does not supply an exact last-frost date for an individual Edenvale garden.

resources.title: Aphids: integrated pest management for home gardens
resources.source: University of California Statewide IPM Program
resources.why: A practical evidence-led alternative to untested homemade pest remedies.
takeaways: Ladybird beetles, lacewings and other natural enemies can suppress aphids.
Broad-spectrum insecticides can kill those natural enemies as well as the pest.
A strong water stream can dislodge aphids from suitable plants.
Ant activity matters because ants may protect aphids that supply them with honeydew [a sugary secretion].
Monitoring pest populations and natural enemies helps decide whether treatment is necessary.
The ecology is useful in South Africa, but US pesticide registrations and product directions do not transfer to SA.

resources.title: Fresh Produce Market Inquiry: final executive summary in the Government Gazette
resources.why: The primary findings prevent stronger claims than the evidence supports.
takeaways: The investigation followed produce from farming inputs to wholesale and formal retail routes.
Agent commissions commonly fell between 5% and 7.5%, with concerns about small farmers’ bargaining power.
The inquiry’s analysis did not establish price distortions at national fresh produce markets, subject to data limitations.
Retail mark-up and margin evidence was inconclusive on profiteering.
It found that retailers often paid farmers more than the farmers would have received through fresh produce markets.

resources.title: Farm-to-Retail Price Spread: December 2025 issue
resources.why: Shows how to analyse the consumer rand without calling the entire gap profit.
takeaways: The issue analyses August to October 2025 across meat and milk chains.
A farm value share compares the raw agricultural equivalent with the final consumer product.
Fresh whole chicken’s reported real farm value share reached 65.16% in October 2025.
The corresponding reported share was 52.54% for class A2/A3 beef.
The price spread covers manufacturing, distribution, wholesale and retail contributions collectively.
These figures describe specific products and periods, not a universal split of every food purchase.

who_pays: Households pay for farming, processing, transport, cooling, spoilage and selling through the food price.
Farmers pay for seed, fertiliser, water, labour and transport before knowing what a perishable harvest will earn.
Small traders carry spoilage and transport costs even when customers cannot afford a price increase.
PMBEJD put its October 2026 household food basket at R5,512.53, while its basic nutritional basket for seven people cost R6,692.25.
Those baskets describe larger low-income households, so neither is a ready-made budget for Sean and Mishka.
who_decides: Farmers choose crops, but access to land, water, finance and buyers constrains those choices.
Municipalities manage public fresh produce market infrastructure, while agents sell farmers’ consignments [produce sent for sale on the farmer’s behalf].
Large buyers set purchasing specifications, delivery requirements and contract terms that small farmers may struggle to meet.
The Competition Commission investigates barriers to competition; the Department of Health sets food labelling rules.
R3337 warning-label rules were still reported as draft in October 2026, so proposals must be distinguished from enforceable requirements.
who_profits: Input suppliers, transporters, processors, market agents, wholesalers and sellers each receive part of household food spending.
Revenue is money received, while profit is what remains after costs, so a large farm-to-consumer price gap is not a profit estimate.
The 2025 fresh produce inquiry found competition problems but made no conclusive finding that retailers were profiteering.
Farm-direct businesses can retain more of the selling price, but must also fund packing, deliveries and customer service.
Informal traders earn livelihoods by splitting bulk purchases into affordable quantities and bringing food closer to customers.
what_it_means_for_us: Start with Edenvale’s produce market and compare it with City Deep’s small-quantity traders before committing to bulk trips.
Compare the cost per edible kilogram, including fuel, delivery, packaging and food that spoils.
Use delivery pages to check Edenvale coverage; a Johannesburg address alone does not establish that a farm delivers to your suburb.
Grow a few herbs and leafy crops first, then expand only when the light, water, harvest and costs justify it.

deep_sections.title: Follow the price, then follow the power
points: A commission market sells produce on a farmer’s behalf, whereas a wholesaler buys stock and resells it.
The fresh produce inquiry reported agent commissions commonly around 5% to 7.5%, with weaker bargaining power for small farmers.
Municipal market fees and agent commissions pay for different functions and should not be treated as the same charge.
A mark-up [increase over the buying price] differs from a margin [share of sales left after a defined set of costs].
For illustration, buying at R10 and selling at R15 gives a 50% mark-up and a 33.3% gross margin before operating costs.
NAMC’s farm-to-retail spread includes processing and distribution, so it cannot identify one firm’s net profit.
NAMC says many market problems identified in 2025 were already raised in its 2006 investigation.
Historical exclusion remains visible in barriers to land, water rights, certification and market access for black and emerging farmers.
Treat a remedy in an inquiry report as a proposed or ordered change whose implementation still needs evidence.

deep_sections.title: Buy together without buying waste
points: City Deep’s trading halls and its cash-based People’s and Unity markets are different purchasing routes.
For two people, loose purchases may cost less overall than a cheaper bulk sack that partly spoils.
A buying club [households pooling an order] can split sacks, transport costs and delivery charges.
Agree who orders, who pays, how produce is weighed and how shortages are shared before collecting money.
A co-operative [member-owned business] has ownership and voting rules; a supplier calling a box a stokvel basket does not prove co-operative ownership.
CSA [community supported agriculture] usually involves an ongoing commitment that shares some farm risk, whereas an ordinary veg box may simply be a recurring retail order.
Ask whether a subscription specifies the farm, seasonal substitutions, cancellation terms and what happens after a crop failure.
No active Edenvale consumer-owned food co-operative was verified in this research, so an informal buying club is a practical experiment rather than an advertised local service.
Farm-direct meat needs a clear farm source, inspected slaughter, traceable batches and a reliable cold chain [continuous temperature control].
Compare usable cuts and bone content before comparing a mixed meat box with the per-kilogram price of a single cut.
Delivery fees and schedules quoted here were visible during research on 15 November 2026 and need confirmation before ordering.

deep_sections.title: Build a Highveld growing experiment
points: Edenvale has summer rainfall and winter frost, so Cape Town’s winter-rainfall calendar does not transfer directly.
A USDA hardiness zone [band based on extreme winter cold] cannot specify a safe transplanting date for every garden.
Fryd gives mid-August as Johannesburg’s last frost, but that broad estimate should not override a local forecast or the conditions in your yard.
Record direct sunlight at the proposed growing spot before buying containers.
Start with food-safe containers with drainage and a suitable growing mix.
Use deeper containers for larger root systems and support tall plants before they become heavy.
In November, beans, basil and summer fruiting crops are options where conditions suit them, but each crop still needs its own sowing and spacing guidance.
Try chard, salad leaves and herbs as repeat harvests rather than expecting a few pots to replace staple calories.
Sow small batches at intervals to spread the harvest instead of producing one glut.
Containers can dry quickly in heat and wind even during the rainy season.
Keep a harvest log with grams eaten, water used and money spent on containers, growing mix and seed.
Treat home growing as partial resilience and skill-building until your own harvest data demonstrate savings.

deep_sections.title: Close loops without garden folklore
points: Compost is decomposed organic material, not simply freshly chopped kitchen waste.
Ordinary compost needs air, moisture, carbon-rich browns and nitrogen-rich greens.
A small cold heap should not be assumed to kill pathogens or weed seeds.
Worm farms use composting worms and moist bedding, with feeding adjusted to what the worms actually consume.
An electric food dehydrator reduces scraps but does not make finished compost.
Open-pollinated seed [a stable variety reproduced through ordinary pollination] is useful for seed saving when crossing is controlled.
F1 hybrids [first-generation crosses] can produce viable seed, but their offspring may differ substantially from the parent crop.
Hybrid does not mean genetically modified, and non-GMO does not establish superior nutrition.
Beans and tomatoes are easier starting points for seed saving than crops needing large populations or extensive isolation.
Dry seed thoroughly and label the variety and harvest date before storing it cool and dry.
IPM [integrated pest management] starts with identifying damage and monitoring pests before choosing a treatment.
Water jets and conserving predators can help with aphids, while broad-spectrum sprays can also kill beneficial insects.
Organic certification describes a production standard and assurance process, not a guarantee that food is pathogen-free or nutritionally superior.

deep_sections.title: Read food claims as evidence claims
points: NOVA [a classification by the nature and purpose of processing] separates ultra-processed formulations from simpler processed foods.
Freezing, pasteurising and canning are forms of processing, so processed does not automatically mean ultra-processed.
The BMJ umbrella review [review of existing reviews] found many associations, but observational data cannot eliminate confounding [other differences between groups].
Relative risk [risk compared with another group] does not give your personal absolute chance of an illness.
Hall’s controlled feeding trial supports a short-term causal effect of the tested diets on intake and weight, but it does not isolate one additive or manufacturing step.
Avoid turning evidence about an overall dietary pattern into a claim that every packaged item is poisonous.
R146 is the existing labelling framework referenced by the Department of Health, while R3337 contains proposed replacement rules.
A legal warning label concerns specified nutrient thresholds or sweeteners, while NOVA concerns processing, so the two systems answer different questions.
Current reporting on R3337 describes regulatory delay and unequal access to discussions, which is evidence of governance problems rather than proof of a secret conspiracy.
PMBEJD’s household basket and basic nutritional basket measure different questions, while a national inflation average can conceal sharp increases in one food.
Use primary reports to test a dramatic headline before deciding who is benefiting or what you should change.
